newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - API's show surprising drop in crude stocks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - API's show surprising drop in crude stocks.

text.p: This week's report from the American Petroleum Institute (API) showed a surprising drop in crude stocks linked largely to a decline in imports that put stocks at near 20-year lows, traders and analysts said.
"The crude drop's a bit of a surprise since a lot of people expected a build in crude related to turnarounds," said Gerald Samuels, managing director of ARB Oil.
Still, winter turnarounds were clearly in evidence, with utilization rates falling by 0.8 of a percentage point, and dipping just below 90 percent to 89.9 percent of capacity.

Crude stocks fell last week by 3.4 million barrels to 286 million -- barely above the 284.8 million barrels recorded in the week ended January 3, which was the lowest level since March 1976, when stocks hit 265 million barrels, API said.
The report was otherwise rather uneventful, showing a drop in distillate stocks and a rise in gasoline stocks, with both at the high end of their expected ranges, sources said.
"The stats were fairly neutral. Heating oil was uneventful. Gasoline was uneventful. Crude was the only thing that was surprising," said Tom Bentz, analyst at ING Derivatives Clearing in New York.

Early evening trade on ACCESS, NYMEX's overnight trading system, showed February heat up 0.25 cent to 67.15 cents a gallon, while February crude and gasoline were steady at $24.24 a barrel and 68.22 a gallon respectively.

The API said gasoline stocks rose by 3.0 million barrels to 199.5 million, fueled in part by a 145,000 barrel per day (bpd) rise in output that was confusing to some sources considering the lower refinery utilization rates.
Distillate stocks, which include heat oil and low sulphur diesel, fell by 2.95 million barrels to 122.5 million barrels, or just 333,000 barrels below a year ago.
Traders and analysts noted the drop in crude stocks was related to imports, which declined last week by nearly 600,000 bpd to 7.83 million barrels.
"It's not very surprising what happened. The drop in crude stocks is probably a function of crude imports," said John Lichtblau, president of the Petroleum Industry Research Foundation in New York.

Responding to question, Lichtblau and others said it was possible imports were lower in sympathy with lower crude demand related to refinery maintenance, but noted it was also likely they were just lower as part of a regular ebb and flow.
"The imports were high last week and low this week," said ING's Bentz, noting imports often fluctuate in such a manner.
-- Oliver Ludwig New York Energy Desk +1 212 859 1633
